source_refs.note: Practice MCQs written from Chapter 3 (PDF 54-74, printed 51-71); not printed in the book. Based on the chapter's text, tables, boxes and worked examples (numericals with changed values); none repeats the chapter exercise. Drafts needing academic review.

blocks.text: Practice MCQs for the whole of Chapter 3 (Circular and Rotational Motion), arranged by the chapter's sections. Each question has one correct answer with a short explanation; numerical questions show the working.

blocks.prompt: 1 When an object moves in a circular path with constant speed, its velocity is:

options.text: constant, because the speed is constant
not constant, because its direction keeps changing

blocks.explanation: In a circular path the direction changes continuously; since velocity is a vector, the velocity is not constant (3.1).

book_ref.quote: When objects move in circular paths, their direction is continuously changing.

blocks.prompt: 2 Which one of the following is given in the chapter as a familiar example of circular motion?

options.text: A stone whirled around by a string
A ball dropped from a tower
A car moving on a straight road
A block sliding down a smooth incline

blocks.explanation: The chapter lists satellites, the Earth's orbital and spin motion, a car on a curved road and a stone whirled by a string (3.1).

book_ref.quote: Satellites moving in circular orbits around the Earth, orbital and spin motion of the Earth itself

blocks.prompt: 3 The angle subtended at the centre of a circle by an arc whose length is equal to the radius of the circle is:
blocks.explanation: If the length of arc AB equals the radius r, the angle at the centre is one radian (3.1).

book_ref.quote: then the angle is called one radian

blocks.prompt: 4 The SI unit of angular measurement is the:
blocks.explanation: The radian is the SI unit of angular measurement and its symbol is rad (3.1).

book_ref.quote: It is the SI unit of angular measurement and its symbol is

blocks.prompt: 5 For a particle P moving on a circle at the end of a rod pivoted at O, the axis of rotation:

options.text: lies in the plane of rotation along OP
passes through P and is parallel to OP
is the tangent to the circle at P
passes through O and is normal to the plane of rotation

blocks.explanation: The axis of rotation passes through the pivot O and is normal (perpendicular) to the plane of rotation (3.1).

book_ref.quote: The axis of rotation passes through the pivot O and is normal to the plane of rotation.

blocks.prompt: 6 The angle Δθ through which the line OP turns in a time interval Δt is called its:
blocks.explanation: Angle Δθ defines the angular displacement of OP during the time interval Δt (3.1).

book_ref.quote: defines the angular displacement of OP during the time interval

blocks.prompt: 7 Angular displacement is a vector quantity:

options.text: only for very small values of Δθ
only for angles greater than 2π rad
never; it is always a scalar

blocks.explanation: For very small values of Δθ, the angular displacement is a vector quantity (3.1).

book_ref.quote: the angular displacement is a vector quantity

blocks.prompt: 8 The angular displacement Δθ is taken as positive when OP rotates:
blocks.explanation: Δθ is assigned a positive sign when the sense of rotation of OP is counter clockwise (3.1).

book_ref.quote: is assigned a positive sign when the sense of rotation of OP is counter clock wise

blocks.prompt: 9 According to the right hand rule, when the fingers of the right hand curl in the direction of rotation, the thumb points in the direction of:
blocks.explanation: Grasp the axis with fingers curling in the direction of rotation; the thumb points in the direction of angular displacement (3.1).

book_ref.quote: Grasp the axis of rotation in right hand with fingers curling in the direction of rotation

blocks.prompt: 10 The direction of a small angular displacement is:

options.text: along the tangent to the circle
along the radius towards the centre
along the radius away from the centre

blocks.explanation: The direction associated with Δθ is along the axis of rotation, given by the right hand rule (3.1).

book_ref.quote: The direction associated with Δθ is along the axis of rotation

blocks.prompt: 11 Which of the following is NOT a unit of angular displacement?
blocks.explanation: Angular displacement is expressed in degrees, revolutions and radians (3.1); the metre is a unit of length.

book_ref.quote: Three units are generally used to express angular displacement

blocks.prompt: 12 An arc of length 1.2 m on a circle of radius 0.50 m subtends at the centre an angle of:

book_ref.quote: Its value in radians (rad) is given as:

blocks.prompt: 13 A point on a wheel of radius 0.40 m turns through 2.5 rad. The arc length it covers is:
blocks.explanation: S = rθ = 0.40 m × 2.5 rad = 1.0 m (Eq. 3.1, θ in radian).

book_ref.quote: which subtends an angle θ at the centre of the circle

blocks.prompt: 14 Three revolutions are equal to:
blocks.explanation: 1 revolution = 2π rad, so 3 rev = 6π rad = 18.8 rad (3.1).

book_ref.quote: the point P covers a distance S = 2πr in one revolution of P

blocks.prompt: 15 An angle of 2.5 rad, expressed in degrees, is about:

book_ref.quote: Consider an arc of length S of a circle of radius r

blocks.prompt: 16 The rate at which the angular displacement changes with time is called:
blocks.explanation: Angular velocity is defined as the rate at which the angular displacement is changing with time (3.1).

book_ref.quote: defined as the rate at which the angular displacement is changing with time

blocks.prompt: 17 A rod turns through an angular displacement of 30 rad in 6.0 s. Its average angular velocity is:
blocks.explanation: ω_av = Δθ/Δt = 30 rad / 6.0 s = 5.0 rad s⁻¹ (Eq. 3.2).

book_ref.quote: Very often, we are interested in knowing how fast or how slow a body is rotating.

blocks.prompt: 18 The instantaneous angular velocity is a vector because:

options.text: it is measured in rad s⁻¹
it is always directed along the tangent
every rotation has a large angular displacement
in the limit Δt → 0 the angular displacement is infinitesimally small and hence a vector

blocks.explanation: When Δt approaches zero, Δθ is infinitesimally small and so a vector; hence ω defined by Eq. 3.3 is also a vector (3.1).

book_ref.quote: So, it would be a vector quantity and the angular velocity as defined by Eq. 3.3 would also be a vector.

blocks.prompt: 19 The direction of angular velocity is:

options.text: along the tangent to the circular path
towards the centre of the circle

blocks.explanation: The direction of ω is along the axis of rotation, given by the right hand rule (3.1).

book_ref.quote: Its direction is along the axis of rotation and is given by right hand rule as described earlier.

blocks.prompt: 20 The SI unit of angular velocity is:
blocks.explanation: Angular velocity is measured in radians per second, the SI unit; rpm is also sometimes used (3.1).

book_ref.quote: Angular velocity is measured in radians per second which is the SI unit.

blocks.prompt: 21 A wheel rotates at 120 rpm. Its angular velocity in rad s⁻¹ is about:

book_ref.quote: Sometimes it is also given in terms of revolution per minute (rpm).

blocks.prompt: 22 A rod makes one complete revolution uniformly in 60 s. Its angular velocity is about:

book_ref.quote: The instantaneous angular velocity ω is the limit of the ratio

blocks.prompt: 23 Angular acceleration is defined as the:

options.text: rate of change of angular velocity
rate of change of angular displacement
rate of change of linear velocity
product of angular velocity and time

blocks.explanation: Angular acceleration is the rate of change of angular velocity (3.1).

book_ref.quote: We define angular acceleration as the rate of change of angular velocity.

blocks.prompt: 24 The angular velocity of a fan increases from 4.0 rad s⁻¹ to 16 rad s⁻¹ in 3.0 s. Its average angular acceleration is:

book_ref.quote: When we switch on an electric fan, we notice that its angular velocity goes on increasing.

blocks.prompt: 25 The unit of angular acceleration is:
blocks.explanation: Angular acceleration is expressed in rad s⁻² (3.1).

book_ref.quote: Angular acceleration is expressed in rad s

blocks.prompt: 26 The direction of angular acceleration is:

options.text: along the tangent to the path
perpendicular to the axis of rotation

blocks.explanation: Angular acceleration is a vector whose direction is along the axis of rotation (3.1).

book_ref.quote: The angular acceleration is also a vector quantity whose magnitude is given by Eq. 3.5

blocks.prompt: 27 For a rotating rigid body, the perpendicular OP dropped from a point P of the body on the axis of rotation is called the:
blocks.explanation: Line OP, the perpendicular from P on the axis of rotation, is usually referred to as the reference line (3.1).

book_ref.quote: usually referred as the reference line

blocks.prompt: 28 The rotation of a whole rigid body can be described by the rotation of its reference line OP because:

options.text: OP has the same linear speed as every point of the body
OP lies along the axis of rotation
OP rotates with the same angular velocity and angular acceleration as the body
OP does not rotate at all

blocks.explanation: As the body rotates, line OP also rotates with the same angular velocity and angular acceleration (3.1).

book_ref.quote: As the body rotates, line OP also rotates with the same angular velocity and angular acceleration.

blocks.prompt: 29 The linear velocity of a point on a rotating body is directed:

options.text: towards the centre of the circle
along the tangent to the circle at that point
away from the centre along the radius

blocks.explanation: The velocity of P has magnitude v and its direction is always along the tangent to the circle at that point (3.1).

book_ref.quote: its direction is always along the tangent to the circle at that point

blocks.prompt: 30 The linear velocity of a point moving on a circle is also called:
blocks.explanation: Because it always acts along the tangent, the linear velocity of P is also known as tangential velocity (3.1).

book_ref.quote: the linear velocity of the point P is also known as tangential velocity

blocks.prompt: 31 A point is 0.30 m from the axis of a body rotating at 20 rad s⁻¹. Its linear speed is:

book_ref.quote: Imagine a point P in the rigid body at a perpendicular distance r from the axis of rotation.

blocks.prompt: 32 A disc has angular acceleration 8.0 rad s⁻². The tangential acceleration of a point 0.25 m from its axis is:

book_ref.quote: Using Eq. 3.7 it can be shown that the two accelerations are related by

blocks.prompt: 33 Two points of a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis are at different distances from the axis. At any instant they have the same:
blocks.explanation: All points of a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis have the same angular displacement, angular speed and angular acceleration (3.1).

book_ref.quote: do have the same angular displacement, angular speed and angular acceleration at any instant

blocks.prompt: 34 Two points A and B are on a rotating disc; A is twice as far from the axis as B. The linear speed of A is:
blocks.explanation: Both have the same ω; v = rω, so doubling r doubles the linear speed (Eq. 3.7).

book_ref.quote: points that are at different distances from the axis do not have the same speed or acceleration

blocks.prompt: 35 The angular equations of motion are obtained from the linear ones by replacing S, v and a by:
blocks.explanation: The angular equations are analogous to the linear ones with θ, ω and α in place of S, v and a (3.1).

book_ref.quote: exactly analogous to those in linear motion if θ, ω and α be replaced by S, v and a, respectively

blocks.prompt: 36 The angular equations of motion (3.9 to 3.11) hold only when:

options.text: the axis of rotation is fixed
the linear speed of all points is the same

blocks.explanation: They hold only when the axis of rotation is fixed, so all angular vectors have the same direction and can be treated as scalars (3.1).

book_ref.quote: hold true only in the case when the axis of rotation is fixed, so that all the angular vectors have the same direction

blocks.prompt: 37 A wheel starts at 5.0 rad s⁻¹ and has a uniform angular acceleration of 2.0 rad s⁻². Its angular velocity after 6.0 s is:

book_ref.quote: Given below are angular equations together with their linear counterparts.

blocks.prompt: 38 A disc starts with ωᵢ = 2.0 rad s⁻¹ and uniform α = 3.0 rad s⁻². The angle it turns through in 4.0 s is:

book_ref.quote: As the other equations of linear motion were obtained by algebraic manipulation of these equations

blocks.prompt: 39 A wheel speeds up uniformly from 10 rad s⁻¹ to 20 rad s⁻¹ with α = 5.0 rad s⁻². The angle turned is:

book_ref.quote: Hence, they can be manipulated as scalars.

blocks.prompt: 40 A fan rotating at 5.0 rev s⁻¹ is switched off and stops uniformly in 10 s. The number of revolutions it makes before stopping is:

book_ref.quote: Assuming deceleration to be uniform, find its value.

blocks.prompt: 41 A force acting on a moving body along the direction of its velocity changes:

options.text: only the speed, keeping the direction unchanged
only the direction, keeping the speed unchanged
both the speed and the direction
neither the speed nor the direction

blocks.explanation: A force along the velocity changes the magnitude of the velocity (speed) keeping the direction unchanged (3.2).

book_ref.quote: A force acting on a moving body along the direction of its velocity will change magnitude of the velocity (speed) keeping the direction unchanged.

blocks.prompt: 42 A constant force acting perpendicular to the velocity of a body moving in a circle:

options.text: changes the direction but the speed remains the same

blocks.explanation: A force perpendicular to the velocity changes the direction while the speed stays the same (3.2).

book_ref.quote: a constant force acting perpendicular to the velocity of a body moving in a circular path will change the direction

blocks.prompt: 43 The force needed to bend the straight path of a particle into a circular path is called:
blocks.explanation: The force needed to bend the straight path into a circular path is the centripetal (centre seeking) force (3.2).

book_ref.quote: The force needed to bend the straight path of the particle into a circular path is called the centripetal force.

blocks.prompt: 44 The direction of the centripetal force on a body moving in a circle is:

options.text: along the radius towards the centre
along the radius away from the centre

blocks.explanation: The centripetal force acts along the radius and always pulls the object towards the centre (3.2).

book_ref.quote: This force always pulls the object towards the centre of the circular path.

blocks.prompt: 45 The angle between the centripetal force and the tangential velocity at any point of a circular path is:
blocks.explanation: The centripetal force is perpendicular to the tangential velocity at each point (3.2).

book_ref.quote: Its direction is perpendicular to the tangential velocity at each point.

blocks.prompt: 46 A ball is whirled in a horizontal circle by a string. If the string snaps when the ball is at point A, the ball moves:

options.text: along the radius towards the centre
along the tangent to the circle at A
along the radius away from the centre

blocks.explanation: If the string snaps at A, the ball follows the straight line AB, the tangent at A (3.2).

book_ref.quote: the ball will follow the straight line path AB which is tangent AB at point A

blocks.prompt: 47 A 0.50 kg stone moves at 4.0 m s⁻¹ in a circle of radius 2.0 m. The centripetal force on it is:

book_ref.quote: For a body of mass m moving with velocity v in a circular path of radius r

blocks.prompt: 48 A car moves at 20 m s⁻¹ on a circular track of radius 50 m. Its centripetal acceleration is:
blocks.explanation: a꜀ = v²/r = 20²/50 = 400/50 = 8.0 m s⁻², directed towards the centre (3.2).

book_ref.quote: is the centripetal acceleration and its direction is towards the centre of the circle

blocks.prompt: 49 A 0.20 kg body moves in a circle of radius 0.50 m with angular velocity 10 rad s⁻¹. The centripetal force is:

book_ref.quote: As v = rω, so the above equation becomes:

blocks.prompt: 50 If the speed of a body moving in a circle of fixed radius is doubled, the centripetal force needed becomes:
blocks.explanation: F꜀ = mv²/r; doubling v makes v² four times, so F꜀ becomes four times (Eq. 3.12).

book_ref.quote: Such force makes the body move in a circle by producing a radial (or centripetal) acceleration

blocks.prompt: 51 For the same mass and speed, if the radius of the circular path is doubled, the centripetal force becomes:
blocks.explanation: F꜀ = mv²/r is inversely proportional to r at the same m and v, so it becomes half (Eq. 3.12).

book_ref.quote: Thus, a force is needed to change the direction of velocity or motion of a body continuously

blocks.prompt: 52 A disc spins at 300 rpm. Its frequency of rotation is:
blocks.explanation: f = 300 rev/min × (1 min/60 s) = 5.0 rev/s = 5.0 Hz (Example 3.2 method).

book_ref.quote: We convert 210 rpm into a frequency in revolutions per second (Hz).

blocks.prompt: 53 A disc of diameter 10 cm spins at 300 rpm. The radial acceleration of a point on its rim is about:
blocks.explanation: f = 5.0 Hz, ω = 2πf = 10π rad s⁻¹; a = ω²r = (10π)² × 0.050 m = 49 m s⁻² (Eq. 3.13 with a = ω²r).

book_ref.quote: what is the radial acceleration of a point on the outer rim of the CD

blocks.prompt: 54 A ball is swung in a vertical circle. At the top point, the required centripetal force is provided by:

options.text: the tension in the string alone
the weight of the ball alone
the tension in the string and the weight of the ball together
the difference of the weight and the friction

blocks.explanation: At the top A, the pull of the string T and the weight w both act along the radius; T + w = mv²/r (Example 3.3).

book_ref.quote: These forces act along the radius at A, and so their vector sum must furnish the required centripetal force.

blocks.prompt: 55 A 0.10 kg ball moves at 3.0 m s⁻¹ at the top of a vertical circle of radius 0.50 m. The tension in the string there is (g = 9.8 m s⁻²):

book_ref.quote: two forces act on the ball, the pull of the string and the weight w of the ball

blocks.prompt: 56 At the top of a vertical circle the tension in the string becomes zero when:
blocks.explanation: T = m(v²/r − g); if v²/r = g then T = 0 and the weight alone supplies the centripetal force (Example 3.3).

book_ref.quote: then T will be zero and the centripetal force is just equal to the weight

blocks.prompt: 57 The speed at the top of a vertical circle of radius 0.90 m at which the string just goes slack (T = 0) is about (g = 9.8 m s⁻²):

book_ref.quote: is swung in a vertical circle of radius r under the action of gravity

blocks.prompt: 58 Curved flight of aeroplanes at high speed is dangerous because it requires:
blocks.explanation: Curved flight at high speed requires a large centripetal force (F꜀ = mv²/r), which makes the stunt dangerous (3.2).

book_ref.quote: Curved flight at high speed requires a large centripetal force

blocks.prompt: 59 When a ball is whirled in a horizontal circle by a string, the centripetal force is provided by:
blocks.explanation: Tension in the string provides the necessary centripetal force (3.2).

book_ref.quote: tension in the string provides necessary centripetal force

blocks.prompt: 60 For a coin placed on a rotating turntable, the centripetal force is provided by:
blocks.explanation: For an object placed on a turntable, the friction is the centripetal force (3.2).

book_ref.quote: For an object placed on a turntable, the friction is the centripetal force.

blocks.prompt: 61 The centripetal force that keeps the Moon and artificial satellites revolving around the Earth is:
blocks.explanation: The gravitational force makes the Earth orbit the Sun and the Moon and artificial satellites revolve around the Earth (3.2).

book_ref.quote: The gravitational force is the cause of the Earth orbiting around the Sun

blocks.prompt: 62 A charged particle moving in a straight line is made to move in a circle by:
blocks.explanation: A normal (perpendicular) magnetic force compels a charged particle into a circular path (3.2).

book_ref.quote: A normal or perpendicular magnetic force compels a charge particle moving along a straight path into a circular path.

blocks.prompt: 63 A 1000 kg car takes a turn of radius 50 m at 15 m s⁻¹ on a level road. The friction force needed between the tyres and the road is:
blocks.explanation: The friction supplies the centripetal force: F꜀ = mv²/r = 1000 × 15²/50 = 4500 N (Eq. 3.12).

book_ref.quote: which is provided by the friction between the tyres and the road

blocks.prompt: 64 On a banked road at a turn:

options.text: the outer edge is kept slightly higher than the inner edge
the inner edge is kept higher than the outer edge
both edges are at the same level
the road is made more slippery

blocks.explanation: A highway is banked on turns: the outer edge of the track is kept slightly higher than the inner edge (3.2).

book_ref.quote: the outer edge of the track is kept slightly higher than that of the inner edge

blocks.prompt: 65 Banked tracks are needed for turns taken so quickly that friction alone cannot provide the necessary:
blocks.explanation: Friction provides the centripetal force itself, not energy (book correction to the Tid-bits box, 3.2).

book_ref.quote: friction alone cannot provide the necessary centripetal force

blocks.prompt: 66 If the applied force on a body moving in a circle falls short of the required centripetal force, the body:

options.text: moves away from the centre of the circle

blocks.explanation: If the applied force falls short of the required centripetal force, the object moves away from the centre; the centrifuge works on this (3.2).

book_ref.quote: If the magnitude of applied force falls short of required centripetal force then the object will move away from the centre of the circle.

blocks.prompt: 67 A centrifuge is a laboratory device used to:

options.text: measure the mass of a sample
separate denser and lighter particles from a mixture

blocks.explanation: A centrifuge separates out denser and lighter particles from a mixture by rotating it at high speed (3.2).

book_ref.quote: It helps to separate out denser and lighter particles from a mixture.

blocks.prompt: 68 In the sample tubes of a centrifuge, the denser particles:
blocks.explanation: Denser particles settle at the bottom and lighter particles rise to the top of the sample tubes (3.2).

book_ref.quote: denser particles will settle at the bottom and lighter particles will rise to the top

blocks.prompt: 69 In the dryer of a washing machine, water leaves the clothes because:

options.text: it moves towards the axis and is pumped out
it moves outward to the walls of the rotating cylinder and drains through the holes

blocks.explanation: The cylinder is rotated rapidly; water moves outward to its walls and drains out through the holes (3.2).

book_ref.quote: Water moves outward to the walls of the cylinder and thus, drained out through the holes.

blocks.prompt: 70 In a cream separator, when milk is whirled rapidly, the light particles (cream):

options.text: gather near the axis of rotation

blocks.explanation: Light particles gather near the axis of rotation and heavy particles go outwards, so cream is separated (3.2).

book_ref.quote: the light particles gather near the axis of rotation whereas the heavy particles will go outwards

blocks.prompt: 71 Artificial satellites are held in their orbits by:

options.text: the gravitational pull of the Earth
the magnetic field of the Earth

blocks.explanation: Satellites are put into orbit by rockets and held in orbit by the gravitational pull of the Earth (3.3).

book_ref.quote: They are put into orbit by rockets and are held in orbits by the gravitational pull of the Earth.

blocks.prompt: 72 If the gravitational pull on a satellite suddenly vanished, the satellite would:

options.text: fly off in a straight line along the tangent to the orbit

blocks.explanation: Without gravitational pull, satellites would fly off in a straight line along the tangent to the orbit (3.3).

book_ref.quote: If there is no gravitational pull, they would fly off in a straight line along tangent to the orbit.

blocks.prompt: 73 A low flying Earth satellite has an acceleration towards the centre of the Earth of about:
blocks.explanation: Low flying Earth satellites have acceleration 9.8 m s⁻² towards the centre of the Earth (3.3).

book_ref.quote: The low flying Earth satellites have acceleration

blocks.prompt: 74 The minimum velocity necessary to put a satellite into orbit close to the Earth's surface is about:
blocks.explanation: v = √(gR) = √(9.8 × 6.4 × 10⁶) = 7.9 × 10³ m s⁻¹ = 7.9 km s⁻¹, the critical velocity (Eq. 3.14).

book_ref.quote: This is the minimum velocity necessary to put a satellite into the orbit, called the critical velocity.

blocks.prompt: 75 The critical velocity of a satellite orbiting close to the Earth is given by:
blocks.explanation: In a low circular orbit g = v²/R (Eq. 3.14), so v = √(gR) (3.3).

book_ref.quote: where v is the orbital velocity and R is the radius of the Earth (6400 km)

blocks.prompt: 76 Using v = 7.9 km s⁻¹ and R = 6400 km, the period of a satellite orbiting close to the Earth is about:
blocks.explanation: T = 2πR/v = 2 × 3.14 × 6400 km / 7.9 km s⁻¹ = 5088 s ≈ 85 min (book correction: not 5060 s) (3.3).

book_ref.quote: the minimum velocity necessary to put a satellite into the orbit

blocks.prompt: 77 As the height of a satellite above the Earth increases, its required orbital speed and period:
blocks.explanation: The higher the satellite, the slower the required speed and the longer one revolution takes (3.3).

book_ref.quote: The higher the satellite, the slower will be the required speed and longer it will take to complete one revolution around the Earth.

blocks.prompt: 78 For a satellite far above the Earth, the gravitational acceleration:

options.text: stays 9.8 m s⁻² at every height
decreases in direct proportion to the height
decreases inversely as the square of the distance from the Earth's centre
increases with the distance from the Earth's centre

blocks.explanation: The gravitational acceleration decreases inversely as the square of the distance from the centre of the Earth (3.3).

book_ref.quote: the gravitational acceleration decreases inversely as the square of the distance from the centre of the Earth

blocks.prompt: 79 According to Newton's Principia, an object thrown horizontally with a particular speed from a sufficiently high place will:

options.text: fly off into space at once

blocks.explanation: Newton predicted artificial satellites: such an object will start revolving around the Earth (3.3).

book_ref.quote: if an object is thrown horizontally with a particular speed from a place which is sufficiently high

blocks.prompt: 80 The orbital speed of a satellite in a circular orbit of radius r around the Earth (mass M) is:
blocks.explanation: Gmₛ M/r² = mₛv²/r gives v = √(GM/r) (Eq. 3.15).

book_ref.quote: This force is provided by the gravitational force of attraction between the Earth and the satellite.

blocks.prompt: 81 If the mass of a satellite in a given circular orbit is doubled, its orbital speed:
blocks.explanation: v = √(GM/r) does not contain the satellite's mass; the mass of the satellite is unimportant (3.3).

book_ref.quote: This shows that the mass of the satellite is unimportant in describing the satellite's orbit.

blocks.prompt: 82 If a satellite at distance r has a speed less than √(GM/r), it will:

options.text: move to a higher circular orbit
come tumbling back to the Earth

blocks.explanation: Any speed less than the orbital speed will bring the satellite tumbling back to the Earth (3.3).

book_ref.quote: Any speed less than this will bring the satellite tumbling back to the Earth.

blocks.prompt: 83 A satellite orbits at r = 1.28 × 10⁷ m (twice the Earth's radius). Its orbital speed is about (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻², M = 6.0 × 10²⁴ kg):

book_ref.quote: is required to hold the satellite in the orbit

blocks.prompt: 84 If the orbit radius of a satellite is made four times, its orbital speed becomes:
blocks.explanation: v = √(GM/r); with 4r, v becomes √(1/4) = 1/2 of its value (Eq. 3.15).

book_ref.quote: Thus, any satellite orbiting at distance r from the Earth's centre must have the orbital speed given by Eq. 3.15.

blocks.prompt: 85 In finding the period of a satellite at height h above the Earth's surface, the radius of the orbit is taken as:
blocks.explanation: The orbit radius is measured from the Earth's centre: r = R + h (Example 3.4); the period uses T = 2πr/v.

book_ref.quote: An Earth satellite is in circular orbit at distance of 384,000 km from the Earth's surface.

blocks.prompt: 86 When you switch on a mobile phone, your location can be tracked immediately by:
blocks.explanation: Your location can be tracked immediately by the global positioning system (Tidbits, 3.3).

book_ref.quote: The moment you switch on your mobile phone, your location can be tracked immediately by global positioning system.

blocks.prompt: 87 Everything inside an orbiting satellite experiences weightlessness because the satellite:

options.text: is outside the gravitational pull of the Earth
is accelerating towards the centre of the Earth as a freely falling body
is pushed outward by its rockets

blocks.explanation: The satellite accelerates towards the centre of the Earth as a freely falling body, so everything inside is weightless (3.3).

book_ref.quote: everything inside the satellite experiences weightlessness because the satellite is accelerating towards the centre of the Earth as a freely falling body

blocks.prompt: 88 A 2.0 kg body hangs from a spring balance inside an orbiting satellite. The reading of the balance (the supporting force) is:
blocks.explanation: mv²/r = mg − F_N and g = v²/r in orbit, so F_N = 0: the supporting force is zero (Eq. 3.16-a).

book_ref.quote: This shows that the supporting force which is acting on a body inside the satellite is zero.

blocks.prompt: 89 For a body hanging from a spring balance inside a satellite, the centripetal force is given by:
blocks.explanation: The weight mg acts down and the normal force F_N up; their resultant is the centripetal force: F꜀ = mg − F_N (Eq. 3.16).

book_ref.quote: or tension in the spring acting upward

blocks.prompt: 90 Astronauts in an orbiting satellite are in a state of:
blocks.explanation: The supporting force is zero, so bodies and astronauts in a satellite are in apparent weightlessness (3.3).

book_ref.quote: the bodies as well as the astronauts in a satellite find themselves in a state of apparent weightlessness
